item.title: Trump’s Super PAC Unleashes Deluge of Ads on Facebook and Instagram
item.description:
President Trump’s political operation has rolled out a major get-out-the-vote program online in the final days of this year’s midterm elections, flooding Facebook and Instagram with ads encouraging Republicans in a number of states to cast their ballots.

Mr. Trump’s super PAC has emerged as the single largest spender nationwide on the two giant social media platforms in recent days, spending more than $1.1. million on Saturday alone. That’s four times as much as the next largest political advertiser that day.

The deluge of digital ads comes as Mr. Trump’s team is trying to boost Republican enthusiasm in the face of the president’s historically low approval ratings. With just two weeks until the midterm elections, polling shows that the president’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries — have threatened the party’s fortunes across the country.

Notably, Mr. Trump’s political operation is aiming its advertising not only broadly at particular states or congressional districts, but specifically at “custom audiences” of individual voters who it hopes are receptive to being pushed to the polls.

A public database of online advertising maintained by Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, shows that 100 percent of the ad spending from Mr. Trump’s super PAC is targeting these custom audiences, which the Trump team provided to the platform.

The ads are running in more than 20 states.

Mr. Trump’s super PAC, called MAGA Inc., has sharply escalated its advertising activity in recent days. The super PAC spent $431,458 on Oct. 14, then $681,107 on Oct. 15, then $822,586 on Oct. 16 and $1,154,832 on Oct. 17, the most recent date for which numbers are available.

The super PAC has run more than 2,200 unique ads just in the last week. Political groups often run large numbers of different ads that can vary in minor ways, to see which are most effective.

Some of the most-viewed ads urge Republicans to vote early. “Beat the lines” and “Do your part,” urge ads running in Michigan, Ohio and Texas that have each been seen more than one million times. Another says, “Don’t turn back the clock,” urging Texans to vote early and declaring that “Democrats broke the border.”

Sagging Republican enthusiasm is one of the party’s key challenges in the final campaign stretch. Many of the tightest contests this year — for both Senate and House — are in more traditionally conservative territory, where Mr. Trump’s political operation hopes to remind voters that there is a consequential election. Operatives are trying to reach particularly those who are likely to vote Republican if they show up.

Also on Tuesday, Mr. Trump began publishing posts on Truth Social urging voters in specific states to vote.

“Early Voting, in-person, is UNDERWAY NOW in the Great State of Maine,” Mr. Trump wrote in one post, with similar messages for residents of North Carolina, Ohio and Iowa, all of which have key Senate contests.

And his super PAC is urging Republicans to head to the polls immediately. Banking votes is a common strategy to help political parties focus their resources more narrowly on those who have not yet cast ballots.

One ad features a photo of Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the two Democratic leaders.

“They’re counting on you to stay home,” reads the ad, with a picture of a hand holding a ballot with red text that reads, “Prove them wrong.”

MAGA Inc. is paying for the ads, but they but they appear online as part of a new Facebook account called Common Sense Voters Coalition.

MAGA Inc. has also begun advertising on Google in recent days for the first time this year, spending $733,000 so far, company records show.

The ads include encouragements such as “Don’t Stay Home,” “Do Your Part,” “Vote Early” and “Make a Plan.”

A spokesman for Mr. Trump’s super PAC declined to comment on the online campaign.

The new digital spending is just one piece of an advertising blitz by the Trump operation since the beginning of September. His allied super PACs have spent nearly $200 million, mostly on television ads, since Sept. 1, according to data from the media-tracking firm AdImpact. Mr. Trump’s team has advertised in Senate and House races in two dozen states, helping give the Republican Party an edge in spending.

Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he planned for the operation to spend more than $400 million in all this cycle. New filings on Tuesday evening will show how much he spent in September.

The spending from MAGA Inc. is not the only get-out-the-vote digital operation on the right.

America PAC, which is funded by Elon Musk, the multibillionaire tech titan, has also been running ads online encouraging people to vote.

On Saturday, the most recent day in the ad database, MAGA Inc.’s spending was more than four times as large as the next closest political advertiser in the country. Next on the list was WinSenate, an offshoot of the top Democratic super PAC focused on Senate races, which spent $289,520 on Saturday.

item.title: A Billionaire Wanted a Trump Pardon. His Family Gave Alina Habba a $50 Million Deal.
item.description:
Julio Herrera Velutini really wanted a pardon.

A billionaire banker from a prominent Venezuelan family, Mr. Herrera faced felony bribery charges in the United States and struck an unusually lenient plea deal in August 2025 for a misdemeanor campaign finance violation. But he felt that reduced charge was still a stain on his record.

So Mr. Herrera deployed his lawyer, Christopher M. Kise, the former Florida solicitor general who was on Mr. Trump’s personal legal team, to help with a plea for clemency. His 27-year-old daughter, Isabela Herrera, who is an American citizen, donated $3.5 million to a super PAC tied to Mr. Trump. But as of last fall, the pardon remained elusive.

Then the Herrera family hired Alina Habba, who had been one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers and at the time was an adviser at the Justice Department. They offered her $10 million a year for four years along with a range of bonuses. In total, including bonuses, she was guaranteed more than $50 million over four years, according to interviews and documents obtained by The New York Times.

Under the agreement, Ms. Habba would become general counsel at Concord Partners, a company that Ms. Herrera set up in late October 2025 in Florida. The company has no public profile and its business remains unclear even to some people associated with the Herrera business empire. Ms. Habba finalized her deal days after the company was registered.

At the time, Ms. Habba was also a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi, overseeing U.S. attorneys. She had an office at the Justice Department and a protective detail from the U.S. Marshals, a holdover from her time serving as the U.S. attorney in New Jersey.

She formally began her work for Concord Partners on Jan. 1. Weeks later, Mr. Trump granted Mr. Herrera a full and unconditional pardon.

The sequence of events raises questions about how Mr. Herrera secured the pardon and who might have helped him. People familiar with Ms. Habba’s contract said they believed that she was brought in to help with Mr. Herrera’s push for a pardon and expressed surprise at the scale of the compensation.

Ms. Habba denied any role in the pardon.

“Any insinuation that my employment — all of which has been vetted and disclosed to the D.O.J. — had anything to do with securing a pardon is false,” she said in a statement.

Ms. Habba was a special government employee at the time, which allows individuals to work for the federal government for up to 130 days and maintain outside employment with conflict-of-interest restrictions.

She declined to discuss her work for Concord.

Ms. Herrera and Mr. Herrera did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did their companies. In a statement, the Justice Department said Ms. Habba did not speak to anyone about a pardon.

A White House official said that Ms. Habba had nothing to do with the pardon and that the administration follows a pardon review process that includes the White House Counsel’s Office and the Justice Department.

In Mr. Trump’s second term, a pardon industry has sprouted up, with wealthy criminals paying well-connected lawyers, fixers and lobbyists to appeal to the administration and its allies in an effort to secure pardons. Many pardon seekers have come to the conclusion that supporting Mr. Trump and his political agenda is the fastest way to secure clemency.

Some people looking for pardons have reported paying hundreds of thousands of dollars or even $1 million to hire people promising access to the president or influence over the pardon process.

For Ms. Habba, the job from the Herrera family came at a pivotal point in her life and career.

She resigned in December 2025 as U.S. attorney in New Jersey after a panel of federal judges ruled that her appointment by Mr. Trump had been carried out unlawfully. Her second marriage was also falling apart.

The arrangement with the Herreras provided her with a new level of financial security. She also found new love. Shortly after the pardon was issued, Ms. Habba started dating Turhan Mildon, a Turkish investor.

They were married last month in a lavish ceremony in New York. The guest list included Attorney General Todd Blanche; the F.B.I. director, Kash Patel; and Will Scharf, the White House counsel.

The couple is now engaged in high-profile feud with Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally. Ms. Habba has accused Mr. Grenell of misallocating a donation from her husband to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, which Mr. Grenell was running at the time. Mr. Grenell has denied her accusations, calling them absurd.

Ms. Habba brought those accusations directly to Mr. Trump, who directed Mr. Scharf to investigate them. The Times has previously reported that the investigation centers on a bank transfer from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company.

Mr. Herrera, who also has Italian citizenship, is a member of the Herrera family, a banking, real estate and fashion dynasty that dates back to the 14th century. The family owns estates and castles in Caracas, Venezuela; the Canary Islands; Spain; and Germany.

Mr. Herrera founded a bank based in Puerto Rico in 2008.

In August 2022, he was charged for his role in a scheme to bribe Gov. Wanda Vázquez of Puerto Rico to dismiss a regulator who was investigating the bank. Mr. Herrera, Ms. Vázquez and a former F.B.I. agent who had worked as a consultant for Mr. Herrera all pleaded not guilty to felony charges.

Mr. Kise, Mr. Herrera’s lawyer, helped negotiate a deal with the Justice Department under which Mr. Herrera pleaded guilty in August 2025 to a single misdemeanor campaign finance charge. Ms. Vázquez and the former F.B.I. agent also pleaded guilty to misdemeanors, disappointing career prosecutors who had pushed for harsher sentences.

All three were pardoned by Mr. Trump at the same time, shortly before they were scheduled to be sentenced for the misdemeanor charges.

In July, Banvelca, the Herreras’ family office since 1781, announced that Ms. Herrera, a member of the eighth generation and the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, was assuming leadership of the company. Neither the news release nor her bio on the company’s website makes any mention of Concord Partners, the vehicle employing Ms. Habba, who now goes by Mrs. Mildon.

Kenneth P. Vogel contributed to this report.

item.title: ICE Says It Didn’t Hit a Biker With a Car. Video Raises Questions.
item.description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Tuesday denied hitting a cyclist with a car in Long Beach, Calif., before detaining him.

But video footage of the moments before the interaction and an account shared publicly by the man’s daughter offer a different story.

Footage obtained by The New York Times shows the moment an S.U.V. driving the wrong way down a one-way street swerves toward an oncoming bicyclist. An officer jumps out, appearing to draw a weapon that is immediately trained on the rider.

The man on the bike, Ricardo Gonzalez, is an American citizen, according to his daughter, Leslie Gonzalez. She has said on social media that her father was struck by the vehicle.

Mr. Gonzalez has worked for the city of Long Beach, according to the mayor, Rex Richardson, who has submitted a complaint to the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, calling for an independent investigation into the agents’ treatment of Mr. Gonzalez and the overall operation.

Mr. Gonzalez had called 911 at one point on Saturday, the mayor also said. He did not have details about how the altercation unfolded, and it was not clear what, if any, interaction Mr. Gonzalez had with ICE agents before the moments shown on video.

Mr. Gonzalez did not respond to requests for an interview, and Ms. Gonzalez, who initially posted about the encounter on Instagram, also declined to comment further, citing concerns about her family’s safety.

After being confronted by agents, Mr. Gonzalez was “tased” and pinned to the ground, his daughter wrote on Instagram.

In the video footage, Mr. Gonzalez can be heard yelling. “You hit me with your car. I’m a U.S. citizen!” he says, using several expletives.

Mr. Gonzalez was later taken to a hospital for his injuries, the Long Beach police said. The police was not involved in immigration enforcement and did not make any arrests at the scene, the department added. It said its officers were called in for backup by ICE, which had reported that vehicles were being vandalized and that a person needed medical attention. The extent of Mr. Gonzalez’s injuries was not clear on Tuesday.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

In its statement, a spokesperson for ICE said the agency had been conducting a targeted operation to arrest a “criminal illegal alien.” The agency did not say whether it thought Mr. Gonzalez was that person. The agency also said its officers had used “the minimum amount of force.”

“ICE did NOT hit an individual on a bike. An individual was arrested after he smashed the mirror of a government vehicle,” the spokesperson wrote.

ICE described the man, whom the spokesperson did not name, as a “rioter.”

The agency said it was investigating charges for “damage to a government vehicle,” the spokesperson wrote, adding that “anti-ICE agitators attempted to impede operations, threaten officers and damage government vehicles despite officers giving lawful commands."

In many previous violent encounters involving ICE, video footage has appeared to contradict accounts by the agency and other federal officials. In January, President Trump and other members of his administration described how Renee Good, a U.S. citizen was killed by an ICE agent in Minneapolis that month, had “weaponized her vehicle” against the federal agent who shot her. Video footage from the scene later revealed no evidence that Ms. Good had run over the agent with her car.

In a similar incident later in January, video footage of the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti revealed inconsistencies between those clips and statements from the Trump administration, including Kristi Noem, who was then homeland security secretary.

Also in January, following an ICE shooting of an immigrant in Minnesota, the agency said the man had violently assaulted a federal officer. Video footage that emerged later did not show such an attack.

Sherman Austin, an I.T. engineer who lives in Long Beach, filmed several videos at the scene on Saturday in the Southern California neighborhood. Mr. Austin, who is 43 and founded an ICE tip network on social media in 2017, said he had been in the area with members of Long Beach Rapid Response, a community group that alerts locals about ICE raids. The group was responding to rumors of unmarked vehicles in the area, which they quickly confirmed.

Mr. Austin said he was warning neighbors when he saw a vehicle speed away down a neighborhood street. He followed that car, which led him to Mr. Gonzalez who was, at that point, already pinned to the ground, Mr. Austin said.

In his videos, Mr. Austin also captured footage of a woman being handcuffed by ICE officers and placed into a car.

“That’s my wife, and that’s a U.S. citizen,” a man is seen yelling in one of the videos, using expletives. The identity of the woman was not clear on Tuesday, and Mr. Austin said he did not know what happened to her.

The neighborhood street quickly became chaotic, as people started yelling at ICE agents and asking local police to intervene.

Mr. Richardson, the mayor, has demanded that ICE agents be taken off assignments during any investigation and that the findings be made public.

“People are upset and outraged, and they should be,” the mayor said in a phone call on Monday.

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

]]>

item.title: New Video Shows Chaotic Moments Before Mississippi Police Shot Toddler
item.description:
Moments before a Mississippi police officer fired at a car this summer, killing a toddler inside, five officers rushed out to a Walmart parking lot in pursuit of two women who were accused of stealing diapers and baby clothes.

Newly released videos show a gray sedan, carrying 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, his mother and another woman, reversing and slamming into a parked vehicle as police officers run toward the car and order the driver to stop.

As the car stops, the officers approach and surround the vehicle before the driver accelerates and lurches left, appearing to travel toward at least one of the officers before passing between two of them. At least one officer shoots into the vehicle.

The chaotic scene in Senatobia, Miss., captured on body cameras worn by two of the five officers and by surveillance cameras, provides the first glimpse of a shooting that has rocked the tiny city and raised questions about whether the officer was justified in opening fire at the vehicle.

The Mississippi attorney general’s office, which declined to comment on the video, announced on Monday that it would not bring criminal charges against the officer who fatally shot Kohen.

The compilation of several body-cam and surveillance clips was first published by a local news outlet, Darkhorse Press. A law enforcement official confirmed its authenticity on the condition of anonymity because the official was not authorized to provide information about sensitive matters. A video analysis by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News showed the footage matched portions of video of the shooting captured by a bystander.

The body-cam footage released Tuesday is from the perspective of two of the law enforcement officers who responded to the scene in June, but not from the officer who fired. It does not show the entirety of the police response, nor does it clearly show Kohen, his mother and the other woman driving the vehicle.

The body-cam footage begins from the perspective of one of the officers, whose identity is unknown. It shows him rushing toward the gray sedan.

The footage then shows the vehicle move in reverse and hit a parked S.U.V. as officers approach, yelling at the driver to stop. When the sedan moves forward, at least one officer appears to be in front of it on the passenger’s side; a second officer also stands near the vehicle, closer to the driver’s side. Both have their guns drawn. As the vehicle approaches them, at least one of the officers opens fire. The officer appears to fire three more times while standing to the side of the vehicle.

Grainy surveillance footage included in the compilation published by Darkhorse Press also captures the moments from more of a bird’s-eye view. In that footage, two women — one holding a child — are seen running toward a vehicle and reversing in it as law enforcement officers chase them.

More video of the incident has yet to be seen by the public. Kohen’s family is scheduled to view it Thursday morning. Veronica Roberson, the toddler’s grandmother, said state officials had informed the family that the footage included surveillance videos from Walmart, along with five body-worn cameras.

Hunter Foster, an officer with the Senatobia Police Department, was placed on leave while state authorities investigated his actions at the Walmart. Although he has not been named as the one who opened fire, Officer Foster is the only officer among those present that day who was placed on leave.

The shooting death touched off weeks of protests and calls for transparency in Senatobia, a city of roughly 8,400 located roughly 40 miles south of Memphis. Activists and Kohen’s family had been calling on the authorities to release police body-camera or dashcam footage.

Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, said she had been holding her son in her arms in the front passenger seat when the driver, Latoya Ferrell, tried to back out of a space and then drive forward. Ms. Ferrell was seriously injured.

In the hours after the shooting, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation issued a statement saying the police had fired at a vehicle when it drove toward an officer, “almost striking” one.

Jerry Mitchell, Julie Lee, Aric Toler and Alexander Cardia contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: In San Francisco, a Family Earning $325,000 Qualifies for Government Aid
item.description:
John Marman and Natsumi Makiyama work in health professions that would put them squarely in the upper middle class almost anywhere else in the United States.

He is a therapist, and she is a pediatric nurse. But they live with their two children in one of the priciest swaths of the country, San Francisco.

They feel squeezed — and perhaps surprisingly, City Hall agrees.

San Francisco now offers free child care to families of four earning up to $235,000 a year, including Mr. Marman and Ms. Makiyama. The city pays half the cost of child care for families making up to $325,000 a year, an eye-popping level that is more than 3.5 times the country’s median household income.

Raising a family in San Francisco, the city with the fewest children per capita in the United States, has never been easy or cheap. But the affordability crisis has soared to new levels this year as the artificial intelligence boom has driven up prices for everything. That has made life even more challenging for young families not working in the tech industry, and city leaders are desperately trying to ensure that those families don’t flee.

The child care help is one way to offset the city’s spiking housing costs, which have shot up 26 percent in the past year, prompting Mayor Daniel Lurie to recently declare a “rent emergency.”

Rents are higher in San Francisco than in any other large city in the country, according to Apartment List. The median rent for a two-bedroom apartment is now $4,640, the site said. The median cost of a single-family home in the city tops $2 million, a figure that these days would most likely buy a small, basic house in need of work.

On the housing front, Mr. Marman and Ms. Makiyama are comparatively lucky. Three years ago, as San Francisco was still recovering from the pandemic and the A.I boom had not yet exploded, the couple bought a 1,200-square-foot home on the western edge of the city for $1.3 million.

Mr. Marman, 36, brings in about $135,000 as a therapist for the city, and Ms. Makiyama, 39, is working part-time so she can stay home with their toddler son some days. Together, they make just under $235,000, qualifying for free preschool for their 4-year-old daughter.

Although they earn good salaries and own their own home, making ends meet just feels harder and harder.

Each month, they pay $6,400 for their home mortgage and $2,200 for two car payments, car insurance and gas, since they are unable to reach their jobs without their vehicles. Cell service and home Wi-Fi is another $300 per month. They put a little each month toward life insurance, their children’s college accounts and retirement.

They spend more than $150 each week on groceries and have become coupon clippers who try to make cartons of milk last longer than they used to and who visit different grocery stores on different days scouting for deals.

“I don’t want to say we’re rationing, but we’re definitely thinking about not using too much,” Mr. Marman said. “Every grain of rice is eaten, and we make sure there is no food waste. I’m the designated garbage disposal for the kids’ leftovers.”

They are saving less than they would like and will probably stop traveling for a while after annual trips to Japan to visit Ms. Makiyama’s extended family grew too expensive.

“At the end of most months, we’re struggling to find extra cash to enjoy a day out with the kids,” Mr. Marman said. “We’re very lucky to receive the benefit for school, but life is just still very tough.”

Without the school help, Mr. Marman said, they would probably have to leave San Francisco, the city where his family has lived for five generations.

Asked what he thought a family of four new to San Francisco — with no government help, no rent control, no trust funds, no foothold of any sort — would need to earn annually to lead a good, middle-class life, Mr. Marman paused.

“I think close to half a mill is the reality, which is absolutely ridiculous,” he said, noting the rest of the country would probably consider a $500,000 income for a middle-class lifestyle some kind of bad joke. “I think they would laugh at us, and honestly I think that’s fair.”

Even Mr. Lurie, the mayor who has fashioned himself San Francisco’s No. 1 hype man, did not dispute the number.

“Yes, it is an incredibly, extraordinarily expensive city to live in and to work in and to thrive,” he said in an interview in his City Hall office. “That’s why 50 percent off at $325,000 is so essential.”

Mr. Lurie, an heir to the Levi Strauss fortune whose mother is a billionaire and whose children attend elite private schools, might seem like an unlikely champion for family affordability. But, he said, any successful city needs middle-class families and the jobs they tend to fill — including nurses, therapists, police officers, firefighters, teachers and bus drivers.

“We don’t want them leaving for the suburbs or for other states,” the mayor said. “We want them here in San Francisco, and that’s what it takes, so that’s what we’re doing.”

The high salaries paid by technology companies, particularly in the booming A.I. sector, have driven up housing and other costs in San Francisco, making it less affordable for everyone who doesn’t work in the industry.

Mr. Lurie has pressed OpenAI and other local A.I. employers to help support city initiatives. “You can bet I am talking to the leaders of those companies,” he said.

But so far, those conversations have been fruitless.

The child care program is funded mostly by unused money from a commercial gross receipts tax passed by voters in 2018 to fund child care.

More than 9,300 children are enrolled at more than 550 private sites, including preschool centers and in-home day cares, and their families are saving up to $36,000 per child.

Families apply online and provide income information, and the city pays the child care center directly. The money cannot be used for private nannies or babysitters. The city spends $238 million annually to fund the program — including paying families’ subsidies, training and paying child care workers and improving facilities.

Mr. Lurie says San Francisco now has universal child care because all families can either afford to pay fully or qualify for city help.

He pointed out that while Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York campaigned heavily on universal child care, New York City does not yet offer it to all children under 5.

“I’ll brag about that all day long,” Mr. Lurie said. (New York City has enrolled more children in child care programs than San Francisco, but given that its population is so much bigger, Mr. Mamdani’s pledge of universal care has been harder to accomplish.)

San Francisco families who take advantage of the child care assistance say that they’re grateful, but that it by no means makes life easy.

Bianca Finley, 32, and Chris Truitt, 36, use the subsidy to pay for their 3-year-old daughter’s preschool. But that is not their only strategy for curbing costs.

They gave up their rent-controlled, two-bedroom apartment in Noe Valley, an upscale neighborhood popular with families, that cost them $4,017 per month. They moved to a studio in the Tenderloin, a lower-income neighborhood, and pay $2,280 per month.

They are documenting the move on Instagram under the handle “The Poor Millennials.”

Both Ms. Finley and Mr. Truitt work in the wine industry, which has taken a beating in the past several years, and together earn $153,600 annually. They said they had grown tired of having a roommate in Noe Valley and of not being able to pay down credit card debt.

So far, they are happy with their decision, becoming experts in space-saving techniques like building a coffee table that turns into their daughter’s bed at night. But sometimes, they acknowledged, it is frustrating trying to get by in the city they love against the backdrop of such stark income inequality.

“We are trying to keep our mindsets focused on: Just because the system around us is broken doesn’t mean we have to be,” Ms. Finely said.

San Francisco is so pricey, even some people working in the booming A.I. industry get City Hall help. Emma Hare, a legislative aide at City Hall, and her husband, who works at an A.I. start-up related to robotics, bring in just over $300,000 per year and qualify for 50 percent off their son’s child care.

Ms. Hare’s policy brain thinks about whether a city’s role is to “help the median resident or have a really strong social safety net” for the poor, she said.

Her mom brain thinks about the opportunities her son will have growing up in San Francisco — the parks, the museums, the culture, the beauty — and has decided the daily stress is worth it.

Mr. Marman has landed on that answer, too. And for now, he isn’t going anywhere.

“We love this city. We believe in this city,” he said. “This is home.”

As a mom raising two kids in San Francisco, I know firsthand how wildly expensive the city has gotten. But I was still surprised when I heard that Mayor Daniel Lurie was expanding the city's childcare subsidies to include half-off for families of four making up to $325,000, a figure that surely sounds sky-high in most parts of the country. In talking to a lot of other parents who live in the city, however, the figure made sense. The nationwide affordability crisis coupled with the city's unique A.I. boom has made daily life in San Francisco exorbitant, and the city must figure out how to keep the kinds of workers it needs to function. Despite it all, I wouldn't want to live anywhere else.

item.title: How a Democrat Positioned Himself to Be Alaska’s Next Governor
item.description:
The man who could become Alaska’s first Democratic governor in a generation — and the youngest in the young state’s history — is a moderate who does nothing in moderation.

Stories of Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’s intensity are already political legend in Alaska. At 13, he became a state organizer for Howard Dean’s presidential campaign, his age concealed by the internet. A mountaineer, cellist and extreme runner, he dropped out of Yale to win a state legislative seat at age 23, and then spent a decade building bipartisan coalitions, conducting legislative business on his phone as he trained for ultramarathons on Juneau’s hills. That phase ended with a freak paragliding accident that broke two bones in his right leg and slowed him down ever so slightly.

Now the bald, bearded, baby-faced Eagle Scout, known in Alaska by almost everyone as J.K.T., is about to be introduced to a national audience at 37. His once-underdog campaign is testing whether Democrats can win in Republican states by building coalitions across party lines without embracing the socialist left.

To understand how, friends say, you have to know Sitka, an Alaskan island town of about 8,000 people tucked between the Baranof Mountains and the North Pacific. Rainy, remote and insular, with no malls or McDonald’s, Sitka is shaped by Indigenous Tlingit people, generations of American fishermen and the legacy of Russian colonizers, whose onion-domed Orthodox cathedral still stands in the middle of Lincoln Street, the main downtown thoroughfare.

“We have 14 miles of road in this town,” said Alana Peterson, a Sitka tribal leader who has known Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins since they were children. “You might never talk to someone, but you hear their name, and you know exactly who they are.”

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins’s three Republican rivals on the November ranked-choice ballot don’t buy the mythmaking. His chief Republican opponent, Bernadette Wilson, has called him a closet socialist, suggested his initials should stand for “just keep taxing” and labeled him “ChatJKT,” accusing him of being beholden to California tech interests like the six Anthropic employees who contributed $372,000 to his campaign. Of the $4.3 million he has raised, 70 percent came from outside Alaska, though he says that he has set a state record by collecting donations from 3,500 individual Alaskans.

“He’s a radical,” Ms. Wilson said at a recent debate. “Alaska cannot afford that.”

Infighting is hurting the Republican cause. Ms. Wilson, the best-funded Republican, has pleaded for her two Republican rivals on the November ballot to withdraw, as has President Trump. They’ve refused — and one attacked her. Meantime, Democrats are in array; Tom Begich, the scion of a Democratic dynasty in Alaska, finished second in the summer’s nonpartisan, top-four primary, and then dropped out and endorsed Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins describes his childhood as “feral,” and his mother, a tribal health doctor, and father, a commercial fisherman, as “anti-helicopter parents.” He sprinted through the woods behind his house to school; traveled by ferry and bush plane to sleep on strangers’ couches for track meets, cello concerts and debate competitions; and “spelunked the storm-water drainage system” with friends for fun, said Roger Schmidt, his childhood music teacher.

At Yale, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins became obsessed with finding the highest point on Ojos del Salado, the world’s tallest active volcano, which has two summits straddling Argentina and Chile. He assembled scientists and climbing partners, found a company willing to loan him $30,000 in global positioning satellite equipment and set off. When a climber’s death closed the mountain, he returned six months later, missing the start of spring classes. His measurements showed the Argentine side was taller by 12 inches.

After he and a friend, Chandler Kemp, found an abandoned camera on Ojos del Salado, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins spent months tracking down its owner, said Mr. Kemp, an assistant professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

During his decade in the Alaska House, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins helped assemble bipartisan governing coalitions that brought Republicans, Democrats and independents together to run the chamber, often in opposition to the very conservative governor, Mike Dunleavy. He championed legislation recognizing Alaska’s 20 Indigenous languages as official state languages. He pushed to add protections for the Permanent Fund — the state’s oil-wealth savings account, which helps finance government and pays annual dividends to residents — from overspending. He expanded voting by mail and eased the hiring of Indigenous language teachers.

Before Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins entered the governor’s race in February, he used a Google Doc to list all the activities he would have to give up, such as serving on nonprofit boards, consulting and his full, regular workout routine. He got his car serviced and did his taxes three months early.

“He doesn’t do anything casually,” Bud Carpeneti, a former Alaska Supreme Court chief justice, said at a recent campaign event. He also described Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins as the “most strategic person I’ve ever known.”

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins is working with consultants who helped elect Zohran Mamdani mayor of New York, which has opened him up to criticism from the right, and he’s running a similarly relentless campaign over a far more vast terrain.

His message is Alaska-focused: stronger public schools; Alaska fisheries for Alaska fishermen; stable state finances; and cheaper energy through oil, gas and renewable power. He has promised a politically balanced cabinet and bristles at the suggestion he’s building a national résumé, à la Sarah Palin, who 20 years ago became Alaska’s youngest governor at 42.

“I really dislike the whole ladder-climber thing,” he said in Juneau this month over late-night pelmeni, a Russian dumpling dish. “People ask, like, ‘Oh, what’s your 10-year plan?’ or “Do you want to run for Senate?’ or whatever, and it misses the whole point.”

His ability to down prodigious amounts of the dumplings, doused in sour cream, vinegar, curry powder and Sriracha, is also the stuff of legend among friends.

Independents make up more than 60 percent of the electorate in Alaska, yet the state supported Mr. Trump three times and last elected a Democratic governor in 1998. Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, whose legislative district voted for Mr. Trump, finished first in the 17-person August primary with 22.5 percent of the vote.

Republicans may be easing his path, a dynamic not lost on Mr. Trump when he pleaded this week on social media: “Now is the time for all Republicans to unite behind Bernadette.”

The other Republicans — Dave Bronson, a former mayor of Anchorage, and Treg Taylor, a former state attorney general — aren’t cooperating.

“There’s three folks up here on this podium that have experience,” Mr. Bronson said at one debate, signaling toward Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins and Mr. Taylor. “There is one that brags that she does not,” he said, looking at Ms. Wilson.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins is promoting endorsements from Alaska Native leaders, commercial fishermen, police unions and Republicans.

“I am a small-business, individual-freedom, mind-your-own-business Republican,” said Rick Halford, a former Alaska Senate president who endorsed the Democrat. “I don’t agree with him on everything, but he listens and he learns.”

After eight years of gridlock between bipartisan legislative leadership and Mr. Dunleavy, who is barred from seeking a third term, Alaska faces chronic budget shortfalls, shuttered schools, a shrinking population, soaring rural energy costs, the risk of rolling blackouts this winter in the Anchorage area, and an economy that rises and falls wildly with global oil prices. Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins compares the moment and the decisions facing state leaders to early statehood or the construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline.

“I want to get back to the Alaska that I grew up with and loved,” he told supporters at a Juneau fund-raiser earlier this month. “We had agency, we solved problems, and we had a sense of optimism that the future was going to be better than the past.”

item.title: Christianity Today, a Voice of Centrist Evangelicalism, Is in Turmoil
item.description:
Last year, leaders of the evangelical publication Christianity Today summoned the entire staff to a hotel ballroom in the Chicago suburbs for a meeting about their future.

The publication’s chief operating officer, Nicole Massie Martin, opened her presentation with a Bible verse from the Old Testament about rejoicing even in dark times, “though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food.” Then Thomas Addington, the interim president, delivered a blunt message: Christianity Today’s reputation as a staid voice of intellectual centrist evangelicalism — embodied by its proximity to Wheaton College in Illinois — had to change.

Christianity Today needed to be less like Wheaton and more like TikTok, Mr. Addington told his staff, according to several people who attended the meeting. Warning that layoffs were coming, he ended his presentation with a prayer. A senior editor left the room in tears.

Fourteen months later, more than half of the 79 employees at that time have either been laid off or resigned, including an editor in chief and four of the company’s longest-tenured journalists.

In interviews, a number of employees who have departed since the meeting in 2025 said that the changes at Christianity Today seemed to be about more than stabilizing its finances. Its new leaders, they believe, are abandoning the publication’s longtime commitment to independent journalism, a record that includes investigating accounts of misconduct by high-profile evangelicals.

Bonnie Kristian, Christianity Today’s deputy editor until last week, described its new leaders as being driven “by fear, by the kind of anxiety about reputational and financial loss that makes bold, interesting, principled journalism very difficult.”

Multiple journalists said that Ms. Martin and Mr. Addington have made attempts to discourage certain articles and lines of reporting based on feedback from their own social and professional circles. One reporter, who was granted anonymity because of concerns over the terms of his severance agreement, said he was instructed this year to slow down an investigation into a faith-based organization that had financial connections to Christianity Today.

“Every journalistic organization has debates about what content to prioritize,” Mr. Addington said. “C.T. is no different.” At the meeting in 2025, he said, he was using Wheaton and TikTok as “metaphors for where C.T. has been and where the media environment is taking us.” The outlet remains committed to independent journalism, he said.

Last week, the magazine’s new editor in chief, Erik Petrik, took down an article that discussed evidence that the popular evangelical writer Elisabeth Elliot, who died in 2015, was bisexual. Edited and fact-checked over the course of weeks, the article disappeared within 12 hours of publication, after receiving backlash from conservatives online.

The next day, the article reappeared with a note from Mr. Petrik saying that it “was not reviewed prior to publication by some key members of our content team.”

Mr. Petrik declined to say whether he would have published the article if it had been proposed under his watch. As the outlet’s top editor, “I will be cautious when facts are few and controversy high,” he said.

Christianity Today was founded in 1956 by a group of evangelicals including Billy Graham, and quickly became the flagship magazine of American evangelicalism.

Of the many Christian publications that flowered after World War II, it was the only one that insisted on “thorough reporting and professional reporters doing that work from the start,” said Daniel Silliman, who broke a major story for the magazine about accusations of sexual abuse against the high-profile evangelist Ravi Zacharias in 2020.

Mr. Silliman was later asked to investigate accusations of harassment against the magazine’s former editor in chief, the uncomfortable results of which the outlet published without having to seek review by its previous executives.

Along with reporting, Christianity Today publishes spiritual reflections, theological treatises and opinion essays that have long served as a bellwether for mainstream American evangelical sentiments. For decades, it generally avoided partisan battles and was read by Christian leaders and churchgoers across the country.

The Trump years upended the landscape of Christian journalism, and revealed gaps between publishers and the pews. Marvin Olasky, the longtime editor of the evangelical World magazine, resigned in 2021 as the magazine shifted from hard-hitting reporting to opinion journalism of the generally pro-Trump variety. The Christian Post, another evangelical outlet, also shifted to embrace President Trump.

Its 2019, Christianity Today made waves when it called in an editorial for the removal of Mr. Trump. It continued reporting both favorably and critically on the impact of the administration’s policies on refugees, foreign aid, gender policy and child care subsidies, to name a few. Russell Moore, a prominent evangelical critic of Mr. Trump, served as its editor in chief from 2022 to 2025.

The new Christian right that embraced Mr. Trump derides the magazine as “woke” and irrelevant.

The magazine’s woes are not straightforwardly partisan. In one case, Ms. Martin, who wrote in Christianity Today that she voted for Kamala Harris in 2024, proposed publishing a response by a group of Latino evangelicals who objected to an editorial by a Trump supporter.

But its issues reflect wider dilemmas within evangelicalism a decade into the Trump era, when many traditional conservatives still feel politically homeless.

“Can you have a centrist evangelical magazine?” asked Kara Bettis Carvalho, a former senior editor who left for The Boston Globe in May. The magazine’s leaders, she said, have “struggled to figure out our audience.”

Christianity Today has also been buffeted by the ordinary vagaries of the 21st-century publishing industry. The outlet has just over 50,000 paid subscribers in print and digitally, down from 80,000 magazine subscribers a decade ago. It increasingly relies on grants and fund-raising to pay the bills.

Ms. Martin, whose academic and professional background is in Christian ministry, was named president and chief executive at the end of last year. Mr. Addington, a former board member who founded an Arkansas-based e-commerce and logistics company, became its chief operating officer. Both immediately became involved with editorial decision-making to a degree that rattled many editors and reporters.

Christianity Today has a code of ethics that emphasizes its independence. “We maintain strict separation (the news industry term is a firewall) between editorial decisions and sources of all revenue,” it reads.

Ms. Kristian, the magazine’s former deputy editor, said Ms. Martin and Mr. Addington had discouraged or tried to dramatically revise multiple articles, apparently under pressure by the articles’ subjects or others unhappy with their impact.

Ms. Martin said she does not have formal oversight over content, but has asked to be notified before publication when something “may cause contention or affect our external brand in any way.” She said she has not intervened in editorial decision-making, but has simply asked questions about planned articles and passed along feedback from outside the company.

The future of Christianity Today is as a “journalism ministry that helps people make sense of the world through a biblical lens,” she said.

“Nicole has repeatedly affirmed C.T.’s journalism and C.T.’s editorial independence even though she’s violating it,” Ms. Kristian said. “In the meantime, Tom has been openly hostile.”

In a meeting in July, according to notes Ms. Kristian took at the time, Mr. Addington said that “editorial independence and autonomy are taken way too far,” and complained that he had no input into what writers were working on.

Mr. Silliman was suspended last fall by the magazine’s editor in chief at the time, Mr. Olasky, formerly of World, over a news article about a lawsuit against a California megachurch and its high-profile pastor, Greg Laurie.

It soon became clear to the reporter that it was Mr. Addington who had initiated the punishment. Mr. Addington told Mr. Silliman and his editor, Kate Shellnutt, that he was going to fly to California to personally apologize to Mr. Laurie for the article, which he described as unfair. (Mr. Addington said he and Ms. Martin offered to meet with Mr. Laurie, but schedules prevented the meeting from taking place.)

At one point, Mr. Silliman recalled, Mr. Addington wondered out loud why so many of his friends said Christianity Today was “feminine” and “woke.”

Mr. Silliman and Ms. Shellnutt quit the magazine in protest in late 2025. Ms. Kristian resigned in September. Mr. Olasky moved up his planned retirement from the end of the year to last week, after a new wave of layoffs in September left him with half his original editorial staff.

“The end of this era for us also represents something bigger about the evangelical movement,” Ms. Shellnutt said. “It’s a real narrowing of where hard stories can be told and where good stories can be told alongside them.”

In a recent virtual meeting with the staff, Mr. Petrik, the company’s sixth editor in chief in less than seven years, laid out his vision for Christianity Today’s next chapter. The outlet would be smaller, he said, but would maintain its high standards.

And, he added, “we’re going to be gentle in our tone.”

item.title: Trump Approval Hits New Low Two Weeks Before Midterms, Poll Finds
item.description:
President Trump’s approval rating hit a new low just a few weeks before the midterm elections, driven down by broad disapproval of his handling of the economy, the war in Iran and high gas prices, according to a new national poll from The New York Times and Siena University.

Just 36 percent of likely voters said that they approved of Mr. Trump’s performance, while 59 percent said that they disapproved. That is his lowest approval rating recorded in any Times/Siena poll. More than two-thirds of independent voters said that they disapproved of the way he has handled his job as president.

Likely voters said that they preferred Democratic candidates over Republicans by 11 percentage points in their congressional districts in the final Times/Siena national poll before the midterm elections, a slight improvement for Democrats since last month. The metric is widely seen as a strong indicator of political momentum.

The national political environment is bleak for Republicans. Americans broadly disapprove of economic conditions under the Trump administration, with three-quarters rating the economy as fair or poor. A majority of voters blame Mr. Trump for the decline: 69 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, 65 percent disapprove of his handling of the war in Iran and nearly three-quarters disapprove of his handling of gas prices, which are above $4 a gallon.

But Democrats still face serious challenges, particularly as they seek to win control of the Senate. To do so they are trying to flip seats in Republican-leaning states including Texas, Iowa, Alaska and Ohio, which Mr. Trump won by double digits in 2024. Other polls show that Democrats and Republicans are locked in tight races in several key Senate contests.

[Follow all of the latest polls heading into November’s elections.]

Still, the deep economic frustration has even broken into the coalition that elected Mr. Trump to his second term. Over the past year, Democrats have improved their standing among men, young voters and Hispanic voters — winning back some voters in those groups who helped propel Mr. Trump to victory two years ago.

Paul Gettings, a Republican who lost his job running a logistics company in June, said that he supported Mr. Trump in 2024 but plans to back Democrats this year. He cited frustration with high gas prices, the war in Iran and what he sees as harsh immigration enforcement in Simi Valley, Calif., where he lives.

“I’m very disillusioned with the Republican Party and how they can continue to support Trump,” said Mr. Gettings, 62, who is unemployed. “He’s turned into a politician just like the rest of them and it’s a lot of empty promises.”

Among all registered voters, including those who are less likely to vote, Mr. Trump’s approval rating was even worse, with 34 percent approving of his job performance. Mr. Trump built his 2016 and 2024 wins partly on the strength of his support among white voters without a college degree, but the poll found that group is about evenly split in its approval of his job, with 48 percent approving and 46 percent disapproving.

[See all of the latest polls measuring President Trump’s approval rating.]

As views of Republicans have declined, public perceptions of Democrats have grown increasingly positive over the last two years on an array of measures.

The New York Times/Siena Poll

Oct. 12-19

Understands the problems facing people like me

Is the party of the working class

Can fix the problems facing people like me

Keeps its promises

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 3,494 likely voters nationwide conducted Oct. 12 to 19. Does not include those who did not respond or who said they didn’t know.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

A majority of likely voters now see the Democratic Party as the party of the working class — a shift from 2022, when voters gave the Republican Party the edge. Voters also see Democrats as more likely to keep their promises than Republicans, a striking reversal from two years ago, when Republicans held an advantage on that question.

And majorities across nearly every demographic group now view Democrats as more understanding and able to fix the problems of average Americans.

“The Republican Party is, if anything, causing more problems for people like me: being Latino, feeling the weight of that kind of prejudice that I think the Republican Party tends to kind of portray," said Vince Cordero, 25, an independent in Oak Lawn, Ill., who said he plans on voting for Democrats this year. “I also think the Democratic Party deserves an opportunity to see if they’re really up to snuff.”

By a 15-point margin, more voters trust the Democratic Party over the Republican Party to tackle the cost of living, the single most important issue to voters. The party holds an 8-point advantage on the economy, an area that has historically been a strength for Mr. Trump. Democrats have also grown their lead since September on who voters trust to handle foreign wars and artificial intelligence.

The New York Times/Siena Poll

Oct. 12-19

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 3,494 likely voters nationwide conducted Oct. 12 to 19.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

But even amid his declining numbers, Mr. Trump has held on to strong support from his base. The vast majority of Republicans, 82 percent, still approve of his job performance and his signature policies, including the Iran war and tariffs.

“People are upset, ‘Oh, Trump put these tariffs on people and now our food costs go up,’” said Sheila Murdock, a retired nurse from Shelley, Idaho, who has already voted absentee for Republicans this year. “Well, yes, but if you look at the bigger picture and what it eventually does, it makes things better.”

The poll also found immigration re-emerging as a defining concern for voters. Ten percent of voters now say it is their top issue this fall, up from 6 percent in September. Among Republicans, almost 20 percent now say it is their top priority — nearly double the percentage who said the same last month.

While Democrats still hold an edge over Republicans in who voters trust to handle immigration — which had long been a Republican strength — that advantage has shrunk since September. Now, 46 percent of voters say they trust Republicans on immigration, 50 percent say the same of Democrats.

Still, the survey indicates that even as Democratic candidates gain support, there is lingering discontent with their party. Just 28 percent of voters said they are satisfied with the Democratic Party, eight points lower than the share who express satisfaction with the Republican Party.

Much of the unhappiness stems from Democratic voters themselves. Forty-three percent of Democrats said they are unsatisfied with their party, compared to just 16 percent of Republicans who said the same about the G.O.P.

Sophia June contributed reporting.

item.title: Calling Putin a ‘Humanitarian,’ Witkoff Thanks Him for Releasing an American
item.description:
Praising President Vladimir V. Putin as a “humanitarian,” the Trump administration envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday thanked the Russian leader in St. Petersburg for releasing an American man held for over four years on what the State Department called fabricated charges.

The release came after President Trump made a direct appeal to Mr. Putin to let the 74-year-old teacher, Stephen James Hubbard, return to the United States. Russia had accused Mr. Hubbard of being a Ukrainian mercenary.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian,” Mr. Witkoff told Mr. Putin. “You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that.”

The Russian leader, who started a war of aggression against Ukraine that has led to the deaths of tens of thousands of Ukrainian soldiers and civilians, is wanted as a war criminal by the International Criminal Court.

Mr. Witkoff’s remarks came at the start of talks in St. Petersburg, where Mr. Witkoff had come to discuss new variants of a proposed plan to end the war that began with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Mr. Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than in a prisoner swap, at a moment when Mr. Putin has scored a succession of victories in winning Mr. Trump over to Russia’s side in the conflict.

In the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has announced that the United States will buy Russian diesel fuel and suspend the imposition of sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act, named for the pro-Ukrainian senator who died this year. Mr. Trump also called on Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, Mr. Putin’s nemesis.

Turning over Mr. Hubbard, who was tortured, sometimes starved and placed in the general prison population in a country where he did not speak the language, came at little cost to Mr. Putin. But the move buys him good will with Mr. Trump, who is arguing that he alone has the relationship with Mr. Putin needed to get him to end the war.

Mr. Trump telegraphed that he had sought Mr. Hubbard’s release, talking to reporters about it on Tuesday, when the former teacher was still in captivity. But Mr. Trump didn’t mention that Mr. Hubbard was being held because Mr. Putin’s government had sought to take American prisoners for leverage.

In recent days, as he was moved out of a penal colony and prepared for release, it became clear that Mr. Hubbard’s value to Mr. Putin had changed. He was now more valuable to the Russian leader as a symbol of the renewed relationship with the U.S. president than as a pawn in negotiations.

Mr. Hubbard’s health is fragile. The Trump administration has pushed for his release since learning of his case, making it a priority, lawyers for Mr. Hubbard said. He will be flown to a State Department facility in Texas for evaluation and treatment.

The decision by Mr. Putin to release Mr. Hubbard came after a tumultuous 12 days in which Mr. Trump has repeatedly sided with Russia and sidelined Ukraine.

Ukraine said the United States had intermittently cut off intelligence sharing; limited its access to Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet service Starlink; and suspended delivery of its already limited supply of Patriot interceptors, the only defense Ukraine has against Russian ballistic missiles.

Mr. Hubbard was essentially abducted by Russian soldiers from eastern Ukraine shortly after Russia invaded and accused of fighting for Ukraine. Russian sentencing documents said he was given the call signs, or nicknames, of “Samurai” and “Ninja,” and that he manned a checkpoint on a bridge over a river.

This was highly unlikely.

Mr. Hubbard, a Michigan native, was living in the city of Izium, near Kharkiv, after a peripatetic life, teaching English for years in Japan and moving for a time to Cyprus, where one of his sons lived, before settling down with a Ukrainian woman. After that relationship ended, Mr. Hubbard opted to stay in Ukraine.

He had just turned 70 when the Russians invaded. His son in Japan told him to keep his head down, but Mr. Hubbard did not seem to understand that the war had started, text messages between the two men showed. Those messages also showed no evidence that Mr. Hubbard had joined the Ukrainian military. He told his son that all was well. He gave daily updates, like when he went to church. He had a hard time buying food, but said once that he bought caviar “for nutrition.”

The Russians said they arrested him inside the home of an acquaintance in April 2022.

Ukrainian prisoners of war who were held with Mr. Hubbard later told The New York Times that he had been repeatedly tortured because he was an American — beaten, forced to stand all day, given little food and poor medical care. In interviews after they were released, the Ukrainians said they feared for Mr. Hubbard’s life.

In October 2024, a Russian court convicted Mr. Hubbard of being a mercenary and sentenced him to almost seven years in a penal colony.

Unlike other Americans held in the Russian prison system, Mr. Hubbard was kept in the general population, his lawyers said. At times, his family had no idea where he was and the U.S. embassy had no access to him.

Mr. Hubbard was designated by the State Department as wrongfully detained in January 2025.

Shortly afterward, Martin De Luca, a former federal prosecutor instrumental in winning the release in February 2025 of another American held by Russia, started working on Mr. Hubbard’s case.

EPAM Law, a Moscow law firm that worked with Mr. De Luca on that earlier release, found out that Mr. Hubbard was being held in the IK-12 penal colony in Mordovia, the southwestern Russian region commonly referred to as “prison land.” In May 2025, Mr. Hubbard was allowed to call his son in Cyprus, Joseph Coleman.

Mr. Coleman, who is a Greek Orthodox priest, wrote a long letter to Mr. Putin in September, making a point of his Orthodox faith, similar to Russian Orthodox, and pleading for his father’s release.

“It’s amazing that he’s been released and we’re grateful to President Trump,” Mr. De Luca said. “I would characterize this as a small dividend on the hard road to peace.”

item.title: Toledo Residents Ordered to Evacuate After Chemical Explosion
item.description:
Nearly 1,000 residents in Toledo, Ohio, have been ordered to evacuate after an explosion at a chemical trucking company on Tuesday led to a leak of hazardous material, city and company officials said.

One person was injured at the scene, Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz of Toledo said in a news conference on Wednesday morning.

The chemical released was glycidyl methacrylate, which is “used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better,” according to a written statement about the incident from MC Transport.

Residents within a one-mile radius of the company’s terminal have been ordered to evacuate. The order initially consisted of a half-mile radius and was expanded overnight. The mayor noted that the area affected was more industrial than residential.

Early on Wednesday morning, Toledo Fire and Rescue also urged people within a three-mile radius of the site to shelter in place, to keep pets inside, close all windows and doors, and turn off any ventilation that might bring outside air inside.

The chemical, when emitted into the air, is a gas, the mayor said, but eventually will return to a liquid state. Emergency response teams have not yet been able to assess the explosion site, he said.

“There’s still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive,” Mr. Kapszukiewicz said, adding that a hazardous materials team would reassess this morning.

The mayor said a foggy morning had made some residents more anxious, as they awoke to a hazy scene outside their windows, causing “a concern that the plume is extending larger than it really is.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump From Denying Gender-Transition Care to Federal Prisoners
item.description:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday prevented the Trump administration from immediately denying certain gender-transition medical treatments for transgender inmates at federal prisons.

The court’s unsigned, unexplained order was a rare example of the conservative-dominated bench siding, at least temporarily, with the rights of transgender individuals. Two conservative justices, Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Clarence Thomas, said they would have granted the administration’s emergency request to stop the treatments.

Under President Trump, the Bureau of Prisons adopted new policies that would prohibit inmates from receiving the care. Three transgender people in federal custody initially challenged the new rules. All three had previously been diagnosed with gender dysphoria by prison medical officials and had been prescribed treatments.

The ruling means that, for now, as many as 1,000 federal prisoners who have been diagnosed with gender dysphoria will continue to receive gender transition treatments that the Trump administration has attempted to restrict.

The lawsuit argued that the administration’s change in policy violated Eighth Amendment protections against cruel and unusual punishment. The policy has been blocked since June 2025, and the court’s ruling means that block remains in place while litigation about the issue proceeds.

Li Nowlin-Sohl, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union’s LGBTQ & HIV Project, called Wednesday’s order a “critical ruling.”

“The attempted denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights,” she said in a statement.

Audrey Cook, the Justice Department’s press secretary, said that while the court’s order is disappointing, it is not the final word on the administration’s policy.

“We look forward to pursuing our appeal in the D.C. Circuit to reinstate BOP’s policy that affirms biological reality,” she said in a statement.

In January 2025, President Trump issued an executive order barring prison officials from spending federal funds on “any medical procedure, treatment, or drug” to address gender dysphoria — a medical condition defined as the significant distress linked to a mismatch between a person’s birth sex and gender identity.

Earlier this year, prison officials issued a policy to implement Mr. Trump’s executive order. The policy permitted other forms of care for people with gender dysphoria, including psychotherapy and medications such as antidepressants.

The prison policy is one of a series of actions by the administration targeting transgender people. The president also directed government agencies to withdraw federal funding from schools that allow transgender athletes to participate in girls’ and women’s sports, and the administration has sought to bar transgender people from the military.

The ban has also been challenged in court, and the administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow the U.S. military to fully enforce it. The case is pending.

At the Supreme Court, the justices in June upheld state laws barring transgender female athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s teams. Last year, the justices also upheld a state law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender youths, rejecting arguments that the law violated the Constitution.

In a narrower case from Idaho in 2020, the court similarly turned down a request from state prison officials to block court-ordered sex reassignment surgery for a transgender prisoner. Justices Alito and Thomas also said in that case that they would have granted the prison officials’ request.

In Wednesday’s case involving federal prisoners, Judge Royce C. Lamberth of the District Court in Washington, has issued a series of rulings ordering prison officials to continue providing medical care to the inmates. Those treatments have included hormone therapy, surgery and social accommodations such as makeup and wigs.

In June, Judge Lamberth found that “no adverse impacts on public safety or the operation of the criminal justice system” would result from maintaining the status quo while litigation continued.

“Denying individuals with gender dysphoria the ability to socially transition or obtain hormone therapy will predictably lead to mental health risks,” he wrote. “These risks include exacerbated depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and self-harm.”

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, asked the justices to intervene on an emergency basis, arguing that the rulings blocking policy were thwarting a step that prison administrators had “determined is necessary to maintain institutional security.”

In defending its new policy, the Bureau of Prisons said that the benefits to inmates of providing such care “no longer outweighed BOP’s other security and prison-administration concerns.”

If allowed to proceed, the government’s plan would mean that inmates who had been receiving treatment would be required to taper off their use of the medication, in a “rapid discontinuation of the hormone intervention.” Social accommodations such as makeup would be confiscated.

Lawyers for the transgender prisoners told the justices in court filings that gender-transition treatment is the only approach known to effectively treat gender dysphoria and that prison officials have provided hormone therapy to transgender inmates dating back to at least 1992.

Prison officials are seeking to “cut off treatment that its health care providers had recommended for decades,” according to lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union. In addition, the lawyers said, prison officials have “not pointed to a single security incident relating to its provision of this treatment over the past 30 years.”

item.title: In Trump’s World of International Diplomacy, Insults Are a One-Way Street
item.description:
The rules of the road when it comes to President Trump’s relations with foreign leaders are clear: He may trash you. But woe unto you if you whack back.

No one knows that better than President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has been through this particular diplomatic wringer more than once. But he got a pointed reminder during a closed-door meeting in Oslo this week with Mr. Trump’s negotiators.

Steve Witkoff, the president’s special envoy, and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, reproached Mr. Zelensky on Tuesday for his sharp comments responding to Mr. Trump’s sharp comments about him, telling the Ukrainian leader that the way he had conducted himself had infuriated the president, according to a person informed about the exchange.

Mr. Zelensky pushed back at times during the discussion as the Americans complained about certain remarks. “I never said that,” Mr. Zelensky insisted at one point, according to the person, who shared details on the condition of anonymity because it was a private conversation. But he clearly got the message. When he addressed journalists afterward, a subdued Mr. Zelensky strained to offer a positive assessment while sidestepping his recent criticisms of Mr. Trump.

“We are thankful to the American side,” Mr. Zelensky said, citing the resumption of U.S. intelligence help. He noted that he had spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio on his way to Oslo, which produced “positive signals from the American side” and that he had a “very constructive dialogue” with Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner. “But,” he added, “it was very constructive between us because all of us want peace: Ukraine, Europe, United States.”

The one-way-street school of diplomacy has worked for Mr. Trump in the sense that his belligerence leaves many world leaders reluctant to cross him for fear of blowback or even, depending on his mood, a fresh round of tariffs. Mr. Trump demands deference while rarely giving any, except to those who accede to his wishes or to those he courts, notably autocrats like President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, President Xi Jinping of China and Kim Jong-un of North Korea.

The contrast between Mr. Trump’s attitude toward autocrats versus democrats was made all the sharper a day after the Oslo meeting, when Mr. Witkoff landed in St. Petersburg for peace talks. Upon securing the release of an American held prisoner in Russia, Mr. Witkoff called Mr. Putin, who faces an international arrest warrant for war crimes, “a humanitarian.”

Mr. Zelensky has been one of the exceptions in openly challenging Mr. Trump at times. But he has to calibrate how far he can push that because his country remains dependent on the United States for its survival as it defends itself against Russia’s invasion.

The Oslo meeting was intended to smooth over the latest rift. Mr. Witkoff stopped in the Norwegian capital before heading to St. Petersburg. Mr. Kushner, who was ill, did not accompany Mr. Witkoff, but joined the conversation via video link.

Mr. Trump’s recent shift further toward Moscow has prompted much speculation that it may be related to the upcoming midterm elections. But Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner went on at length during their conversation with Mr. Zelensky to deny any connection to domestic politics, according to the person informed about the session.

Mr. Zelensky had two friends with him for the encounter: his host, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store of Norway, and the visiting President Alexander Stubb of Finland. Both of them have been strong backers of Ukraine and like most European leaders do not share Mr. Trump’s tilt toward Russia, but at the same time labor not to rile him unnecessarily.

“I’m happy that we were able to get together today to straighten out a few things and to agree that what matters now is to look ahead,” Mr. Store said. “There’s nothing to gain from digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago. We now really have to be focused on what lies ahead.”

Mr. Stubb expressed hope that the back-and-forth with Washington would now end. “Today was a success and tomorrow is a new day and hopefully we don’t do any backtracking,” he said.

Mr. Store and Mr. Stubb organized the meeting in Oslo in hopes of getting peace negotiations back on track. The notion that Mr. Witkoff would have gone to Russia to meet with Mr. Putin without seeing Mr. Zelensky first would have resulted in terrible optics, two European officials said. The meeting in Oslo would not fully resolve the fundamental issues, they added, but there is no real alternative to American leadership.

The White House did not immediately comment on the Oslo meeting. An American close to the talks said that the participants had a frank but respectful exchange that allowed them “to clear the air” and move forward. Mr. Zelensky’s public criticism of Mr. Trump may serve his own short-term political objectives, the American warned, but is ultimately counterproductive to Ukraine’s longer-term goals of ending the war.

This has been the calculation that many world leaders have had to make, particularly in Mr. Trump’s second term — when to respond in kind when the American president lashes out and when to swallow pride in the interest of not poking the bear.

For years, presidents and prime ministers of allied nations went out of their way to avoid angering Mr. Trump, who prefers escalation over conciliation. But in recent months, especially since his threats to take over Greenland last winter, leaders have shown less submissiveness and more willingness to stand firm.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada has led the way with his defiance of Mr. Trump’s attempts to strong-arm America’s northern neighbor into making trade concessions. Rather than back down, as leaders often did in Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Carney decided “to hit back” and slapped on dollar-for-dollar tariffs in retaliation.

Mr. Zelensky’s situation, however, is more complicated. Mr. Trump has been predisposed against Ukraine since his first term, convinced by advisers that Kyiv meddled in the 2016 election against him, an unfounded assertion that intelligence agencies have called Russian disinformation. His effort in 2019 to pressure Mr. Zelensky into opening an investigation into his Democratic rival, Joseph R. Biden Jr., led to Mr. Trump’s first impeachment for abuse of power.

The tone for the second term was set shortly after Mr. Trump returned to power last year and berated Mr. Zelensky in an explosive Oval Office meeting. Mr. Zelensky demonstrated at the time that he was unafraid to stand up to the president. But under coaching from European leaders and congressional allies, Mr. Zelensky has since mostly sought to avoid direct confrontations.

The past two weeks made that more difficult as Mr. Trump, who has long had a convivial relationship with Mr. Putin, pivoted even more dramatically in Moscow’s direction. Among other things, Mr. Trump and his team have struck a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel, lifted some sanctions and exempted Russia from others included in legislation that he just signed, curbed some intelligence and satellite assistance for Kyiv, delayed the delivery of interceptors and worked to broker an agreement to sell lucrative Russian oil assets to people with ties to Mr. Trump’s circle.

Mr. Trump has lashed out repeatedly against Mr. Zelensky in recent days, calling it “disgraceful” for Ukraine to strike Russian oil refineries and insisting that it “damn well stop.” He once again blamed Mr. Zelensky for the war that Mr. Putin started and said that “Russia has been fine” even as intensifying Russian missile and drone barrages are killing more civilians in Ukraine than at any time since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

Mr. Trump went so far as to demand that Ukraine “get a new president” instead of Mr. Zelensky. By contrast, he has had no tough words for Mr. Putin, saying that he did not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

It goes well beyond diplomatic protocol to explicitly push for the ouster of the leader of a fellow democracy. But when Mr. Zelensky responded by calling the diesel move a “weak decision,” suggesting that he felt “betrayed” and indicating that it seemed that Washington was trying “to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Mr. Trump adopted the role of the aggrieved party.

Just hours before the Oslo meeting, he again lay the responsibility for making peace on Ukraine rather than Mr. Putin, who could end the war tomorrow by stopping his attacks on his neighbor. “Zelensky has to want to settle this war,” Mr. Trump told reporters in Washington. “And if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing.”

Mr. Trump’s assertion that Mr. Zelensky, rather than Mr. Putin, is the obstacle to peace offends Ukrainians and Europeans alike. Mr. Zelensky emphasized in Oslo that, after all, his people are the ones under bombardment.

“We are losing people, and because Russia attacks, we’re losing people and time, and it’s a pity because our children don’t have real life, childhood, and all the people, to be honest,” he said. “That’s why we need to end this war as quick as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us.”
